body_html:
The Spanish mistakes learners make are remarkably predictable. After ten years of translating between English and Spanish, and many more years reading learners’ messages, emails and essays, I see the same errors again and again. They are not signs of a bad memory. They come from habits carried over from English: assuming nouns have no gender, translating prepositions one by one, using one verb for “to be”, and trusting words that look familiar. This guide puts every common mistake in one place, grouped into families. For each one you get the wrong version, the right version, the reason behind it and a quick fix, plus a link to a full guide with conversations and a quiz.

Key takeaways
  • Most Spanish mistakes come from English structures carried directly into Spanish.
  • They fall into four families: grammar and structure, word choice, meaning and manners, and writing.
  • Beginners should fix gender, articles, gustar and age first; the rest can wait.
  • Fix one family at a time, using whole sentences rather than rules alone.
  • Mistakes are normal. People you talk to care far more that you try.
{{toc}}

Why Spanish mistakes are so predictable

Your first language works like a template. When Spanish behaves like English, you move quickly. When it doesn’t, your brain quietly falls back on the English pattern, and a mistake appears. That is why learners from different first languages make different mistakes, and why learners whose first language is English tend to make the same ones.

The trouble spots fall into two groups. The first is features English simply doesn’t have: grammatical gender, the personal a, two verbs for “to be” and verb endings that make subject pronouns optional. The second is features English handles differently: word order, prepositions, the “backwards” structure of gustar and the way Spanish describes hunger, age and feelings with tener.

This is good news. Because the mistakes are not random, you can fix them systematically, one family at a time, instead of hoping they disappear with time.

Which mistakes to fix first

Not every mistake matters equally. Some make you sound slightly foreign; others change your meaning or make you hard to understand. Here is the order I recommend.

Your levelFix these firstWhy
Beginner (A1–A2)Noun gender, articles, gustar, saying your age, accent marks on common wordsThey appear in almost every sentence you say.
Intermediate (B1)Prepositions, ser vs estar, word order and pronouns, double negatives, false friendsThey are the difference between “understood” and “natural”.
Upper intermediate (B2+)Literal translation, politeness and register, punctuation, capitalizationThey are what native readers notice in emails and formal writing.

If you are not sure of your level, start at the top and move down. Each section below follows the same pattern: what learners say, what Spanish speakers say, and the one idea that fixes it.

Grammar and structure mistakes

1. Noun gender

Wrong: la problema, el mano, la día. Right: el problema, la mano, el día.

Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and the adjectives and articles around it have to agree. The rule that most nouns ending in -o are masculine and most ending in -a are feminine works well, but the exceptions are some of the most frequent words in the language: el mapa, el idioma, el sistema, la foto, la moto, la radio. There is also a famous trap: el agua uses el for sound reasons but is feminine, so you say el agua fría.

Quick fix: never learn a noun on its own. Learn la mano, not mano. Full guide: {{link:spanish-gender-mistakes|Spanish gender mistakes}}.

2. Articles

Wrong: Gente es amable. Soy un profesor. Hablo el español. Right: La gente es amable. Soy profesor. Hablo español.

Spanish uses the definite article where English leaves it out, especially when talking about things in general: Me encanta la música (I love music), Los perros son leales (Dogs are loyal). At the same time, Spanish drops un and una before an unmodified profession, religion or nationality. You also don’t need an article after hablar with a language.

Quick fix: general statements take el, la, los, las; jobs after ser take nothing. Full guide: {{link:spanish-article-mistakes|Spanish article mistakes}}.

3. Word order and object pronouns

Wrong: una roja casa, Veo lo., Le lo di. Right: una casa roja, Lo veo., Se lo di.

Most adjectives follow the noun in Spanish. A few change meaning depending on position: un gran hombre is a great man, un hombre grande is a big one. Object pronouns go before a conjugated verb, or attach to an infinitive: Lo quiero ver or Quiero verlo. When two third-person pronouns meet, le or les becomes se.

Quick fix: say the noun first, then describe it. Full guide: {{link:spanish-word-order|Spanish word order}}, and for choosing the pronoun itself, {{link:lo-vs-le|lo vs le}}.

4. Prepositions

Wrong: Depende en ti. Busco para mis llaves. Visité mi abuela. Right: Depende de ti. Busco mis llaves. Visité a mi abuela.

Prepositions rarely translate one to one. “Depend on” is depender de, “think about” is pensar en, “dream about” is soñar con, “marry” is casarse con and “fall in love with” is enamorarse de. Some English phrasal verbs need no preposition at all in Spanish: buscar (look for), esperar (wait for), escuchar (listen to). And when the direct object is a specific person or a pet, Spanish adds the personal a.

Quick fix: learn each verb with its preposition as one unit. Full guide: {{link:spanish-preposition-mistakes|Spanish preposition mistakes}}. The biggest preposition question of all has its own guide: {{link:por-vs-para|por vs para}}.

5. Gustar

Wrong: Yo gusto los perros. Ana gusta bailar. Right: Me gustan los perros. A Ana le gusta bailar.

Gustar means “to be pleasing to”. The thing you like is the grammatical subject, so the verb agrees with it, not with you: me gusta el libro, me gustan los libros. Be careful with Me gustas. It means “I like you” in a romantic sense, and ¿Te gusto? means “Do you like me?” in the same way. Verbs like encantar, interesar and doler work exactly the same way.

Quick fix: ask “what is pleasing?” and make the verb agree with that. Full guide: {{link:how-to-use-gustar|how to use gustar}}.

6. Ser and estar

Wrong: Soy cansado. La fiesta está en mi casa. Right: Estoy cansado. La fiesta es en mi casa.

Spanish has two verbs for “to be”, and choosing the wrong one can change your meaning: Soy aburrido (I’m boring) vs Estoy aburrido (I’m bored), Es listo (he’s clever) vs Está listo (he’s ready). The usual shortcut is that ser is for identity and estar for states and location, but events are an exception: where a party or meeting takes place uses ser.

Quick fix: ask “is this what it is, or how it is right now?” Full guide: {{link:ser-vs-estar|ser vs estar}}.

7. Overusing subject pronouns and possessives

Wrong: Yo trabajo en un banco. Yo vivo en Dallas. Yo tengo dos hijos. Me lavo mis manos. Right: Trabajo en un banco, vivo en Dallas y tengo dos hijos. Me lavo las manos.

Spanish verb endings already tell you who is acting, so repeating yo in every sentence sounds heavy and slightly insistent. Use the pronoun for contrast or emphasis: Yo trabajo y él estudia. In the same way, with body parts and clothing Spanish uses the article, because the reflexive pronoun already shows whose hands they are.

Quick fix: drop the pronoun unless you are contrasting two people. Full guide: {{link:subject-pronouns-in-spanish|subject pronouns in Spanish}}.

8. Double negatives

Wrong: Veo nada. No viene alguien. Right: No veo nada. No viene nadie. or Nadie viene.

In standard English, two negatives cancel out. In Spanish they reinforce each other, and they are required. If a negative word like nada, nadie or nunca comes after the verb, you need no before it. If it comes first, you don’t: Nunca llueve aquí.

Quick fix: negative word after the verb means no in front. Full guide: {{link:double-negatives-in-spanish|double negatives in Spanish}}.

9. Plurals

Wrong: La gente son amables. los lápizes. Right: La gente es amable. los lápices.

The plural rules are simple, but the details trip learners up: -z becomes -ces, accents appear or disappear (canción, canciones), days like el lunes never change, and la gente is singular. Full guide: {{link:spanish-plural-mistakes|Spanish plural mistakes}}.

{{image:2}}

Word choice mistakes

9. One English word, two Spanish words

A huge share of word-choice mistakes happen because English uses one word where Spanish uses two. These are the pairs I correct most often:

EnglishSpanishThe rule in one line
askpedir / preguntarAsk for something vs ask a question. {{link:pedir-vs-preguntar|Guide}}
knowsaber / conocerFacts and skills vs people and places. {{link:saber-vs-conocer|Guide}}
bring / taketraer / llevarToward the speaker vs away from the speaker. {{link:llevar-vs-traer|Guide}}
playjugar / tocarGames and sports vs instruments. {{link:tocar-vs-jugar|Guide}}
butpero / sinoAdding a contrast vs correcting a negative. {{link:pero-vs-sino|Guide}}
good / wellbueno / bienDescribes a noun vs describes an action. {{link:bueno-vs-bien|Guide}}

There are more than thirty of these pairs, and I’ve collected them all, each with a rule and a quiz, in {{link:spanish-confusing-words|Spanish confusing words}}.

10. False friends

Wrong: Realicé que era tarde. Fui a la librería a sacar un libro. Right: Me di cuenta de que era tarde. Fui a la biblioteca a sacar un libro.

False friends look like English words but mean something else. Realizar means to carry out, asistir means to attend, librería is a bookstore (a library is a biblioteca), actualmente means currently, éxito means success, and molestar means to bother. Because they look so familiar, learners rarely stop to check them.

Quick fix: be suspicious of any Spanish word that looks too easy. Full guide: {{link:spanish-false-friends|Spanish false friends}}. The opposite case, words that really do mean the same, is covered in {{link:english-spanish-cognates|English–Spanish cognates}}.

11. Forcing an English word into Spanish

Some English words have no single Spanish equivalent, so learners invent one or borrow the English. “Cozy” might be acogedor, “awkward” could be incómodo or raro, and “I’m excited” depends on the context. The fix is to translate the situation, not the word. Full guide: {{link:english-words-that-dont-translate-to-spanish|English words that don’t translate to Spanish}}.

Meaning and manners mistakes

12. Translating word for word

Wrong: Estoy hambre. Hace sentido. Tuve un buen tiempo. Right: Tengo hambre. Tiene sentido. La pasé muy bien.

Spanish describes many physical states with tener: hunger, thirst, cold, heat, sleepiness, fear and being in a hurry. Idioms almost never transfer: “a piece of cake” is pan comido, and “it’s raining cats and dogs” is está lloviendo a cántaros. In Spain you will hear me lo pasé bien instead of the Mexican la pasé bien.

Quick fix: ask how a Spanish speaker would describe the moment, not how to translate your sentence. Full guide: {{link:literal-translation-mistakes-spanish|literal translation mistakes in Spanish}}.

13. Saying your age

Wrong: Soy 30 años. Tengo 30 anos. Right: Tengo 30 años.

Age uses tener, not ser, and the ñ matters: años means years, while the word without it means something you would never want to say at a birthday party. Full guide: {{link:how-to-say-your-age-in-spanish|how to say your age in Spanish}}.

14. Embarrassing slips

A few mistakes are memorable because they produce a laugh or a blush. Estoy embarazada means “I’m pregnant”, not “I’m embarrassed” (try ¡Qué vergüenza! instead). Estoy caliente has a sexual meaning when talking about a person, so say tengo calor when you are hot. Excitado is similar, and coger is vulgar in Mexico and much of Latin America, though harmless in Spain. Full guide: {{link:embarrassing-spanish-mistakes|embarrassing Spanish mistakes}}.

15. Politeness and register

Too blunt: Quiero un café. Dame la cuenta. Natural: ¿Me da un café, por favor? ¿Me trae la cuenta, por favor?

Spanish is not ruder or more polite than English, but it signals politeness in different places. Greeting before asking (Buenos días when you walk into a store), choosing usted with strangers and older people, and softening requests with ¿Me da…? or Quisiera… all matter. Full guides: {{link:spanish-politeness-mistakes|Spanish politeness mistakes}}, {{link:tu-vs-usted|tú vs usted}} and {{link:polite-requests-in-spanish|polite requests in Spanish}}.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Writing mistakes

16. Accent marks

Accent marks are not decoration. They change meaning: si (if) and sí (yes), tu (your) and tú (you), el (the) and él (he), esta (this) and está (is), papa (potato) and papá (dad). Question words carry an accent too: ¿Qué?, ¿Cómo?, ¿Dónde?. Full guide: {{link:spanish-accent-marks|Spanish accent marks}}, with the most confused pairs in {{link:si-vs-si|si vs sí}}, {{link:tu-vs-tu|tu vs tú}} and {{link:esta-vs-esta|esta vs está}}.

17. Punctuation

Wrong: Cómo estás? Hola cómo estás? Right: ¿Cómo estás? Hola, ¿cómo estás?

Spanish opens questions and exclamations with inverted marks, and they surround only the question part of the sentence. Dialogue in novels uses a long dash instead of quotation marks. Full guide: {{link:spanish-punctuation-rules|Spanish punctuation rules}}.

18. Capitalization

Wrong: El Lunes estudio Español con mi amigo Mexicano. Right: El lunes estudio español con mi amigo mexicano.

Days of the week, months, languages and nationalities are lowercase in Spanish. Book and movie titles capitalize only the first word and proper names: Cien años de soledad. Full guide: {{link:spanish-capitalization-rules|Spanish capitalization rules}}.

The Spanish mistakes I see most as a translator

Learners’ textbook mistakes are only part of the picture. In my translation work, especially with Spanish written in the United States, I keep meeting a different kind of error: sentences where every word is Spanish but the structure is English. These calques are understandable in conversation, but they stand out in emails, applications and anything formal.

  • Aplicar para un trabajo → solicitar un empleo or postularse a un puesto
  • Llamar para atrás → devolver la llamada
  • Hacer sentido → tener sentido
  • En orden de (in order to) → para
  • Estoy excitado por el viaje → Estoy muy emocionado por el viaje

Many bilingual speakers use some of these every day, and in relaxed conversation that is perfectly fine; I wrote about why in {{link:code-switching-english-spanish|code-switching between English and Spanish}}. But if you are writing to someone you don’t know, choose the standard form. For doubtful cases, the Diccionario panhispánico de dudas from the Real Academia Española is the reference I check myself.

{{image:3}}

How to fix your Spanish mistakes for good

1. Work on one family at a time

Spend a week on gender, then a week on prepositions. Trying to fix everything at once fixes nothing. Each guide linked above ends with a quiz, so you can check yourself before moving on.

2. Notice, then collect

When you see the correct form in real Spanish, save the whole sentence. Over time, the correct version simply sounds right and the wrong one sounds strange. I describe a simple routine in {{link:sentence-mining-spanish|sentence mining}}.

3. Read lots of natural Spanish

Mistakes fade fastest through exposure. Reading bilingual books lets you compare English and Spanish structures side by side, which is exactly where these mistakes live. See {{link:parallel-text-reading|parallel text reading}} and {{link:comprehensible-input-spanish|comprehensible input}}.

4. Ask for corrections

Tell Spanish-speaking friends: Corrígeme si me equivoco, por favor (Please correct me if I make a mistake). Most people will be happy to help, but only if you ask. The Centro Virtual Cervantes is also a reliable free resource for grammar questions.

5. Check your writing with a short list

Before you send an important message, read it once looking only for these five things: noun gender and agreement, accent marks, the personal a, opening question marks and capital letters on days, months and languages. It takes thirty seconds and catches most errors.

Final thoughts

The mistakes Spanish learners make are a map of where the two languages differ. Every mistake on this page is one I have seen hundreds of times, and every one of them can be fixed. Pick one family, read its guide, take the quiz, then come back for the next. And remember: speaking with mistakes is always better than staying silent.

faq.q: What are the most common Spanish mistakes?
faq.a: Noun gender (la problema), the structure of gustar (yo gusto), ser vs estar, prepositions (depender en), literal translation (estoy hambre), adjective order, missing double negatives and missing accent marks.

faq.q: Why do learners make the same mistakes in Spanish?
faq.a: Because they carry English structures into Spanish, especially where Spanish has features English lacks, such as grammatical gender, the personal a and two verbs for “to be”.

faq.q: Which Spanish mistakes should beginners fix first?
faq.a: Noun gender and articles, the structure of gustar, saying your age with tener, and accent marks on very common words like sí, tú and está. They appear in almost every sentence.

faq.q: Is it rude to make mistakes in Spanish?
faq.a: No. Spanish speakers are generally patient and pleased that you are trying. The only mistakes that can cause real awkwardness are a few false friends, such as embarazada and estoy caliente, and using tú in very formal situations.

faq.q: Do native Spanish speakers make these mistakes too?
faq.a: Some of them, yes. Spelling pairs such as haber and a ver, or porque and por qué, trip up native speakers too. Gender and gustar mistakes, on the other hand, are typical of learners.

faq.q: How can I stop making mistakes in Spanish?
faq.a: Focus on one mistake family at a time, collect correct example sentences, read lots of natural Spanish and ask people you talk to to correct you.
